framework_name: Comprehensive TEKS Forest Literacy Learning Architecture
state_standards_basis: Texas Essential Knowledge and Skills (TEKS) - Revised 2024-2025 Science, Mathematics, Social Studies, ELAR, Fine Arts, Health
national_framework_basis: Project Learning Tree (PLT) Forest Literacy Framework (Themes 1-4)

nodes.title: Parts of a Tree: Roots, Trunk, Crown & Bark
nodes.subject: Science
learning_objectives: Identify and label the four primary anatomical structures of a tree: roots, trunk, branches/crown, and leaves/bark.
Describe how roots absorb water and anchor the tree in soil.
Explain how bark functions like human skin to protect the tree from heat and insects.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Tree Hugger Sensory Anatomy Tour
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students partner up to touch, inspect, and sketch the texture of native Honey Mesquite bark, look for surface root anchors, and observe leaf clusters in the canopy.

formative_check.question: Which part of the tree acts like a giant sponge and anchor beneath the soil?
options: The green leaves
The root system
The upper branches
The outer bark
formative_check.explanation: Roots grow deep into the ground to anchor the tree securely and drink water and nutrients from the soil.

citations: Project Learning Tree (2020) Theme 1: Concept 1.A.1
Texas A&M Forest Service: Trees of Texas Guide

nodes.title: Leaf Shapes, Textures & Simple Patterns
nodes.subject: Science
learning_objectives: Sort fallen leaves by shape (oval, heart, compound bipinnate) and margin (smooth vs toothed).
Observe how desert-adapted native trees like Mesquite have tiny compound leaflets to prevent water loss in South Texas heat.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Fallen Leaf Scavenger Sort
equipment: Sorting mat (Smooth vs Rough, Big vs Small)
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students collect 5 fallen leaves from the ground (never picking living leaves) and sort them into comparative categories.

formative_check.question: Why do Honey Mesquite trees in South Texas have lots of tiny leaflets instead of one giant leaf?
options: To hide from birds
To conserve water and stay cool in hot weather
To catch heavier rain
Because they are baby trees
formative_check.explanation: Tiny leaflets reduce water loss from desert evaporation and allow cooling breezes to pass through easily.

citations: TFS Trees of Texas Leaf Key
PLT Activity 64: Looking at Leaves

nodes.title: Who Lives in the Tree? Animal & Insect Homes
nodes.subject: Science
learning_objectives: Identify at least three living organisms that rely on campus trees for food, shelter, or nesting (e.g., Green Jays, cicadas, honeybees).
Explain the difference between living organisms (biotic) and non-living elements (abiotic) in a microforest habitat.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Microforest Creature Detective
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students quietly observe the canopy for 10 minutes, logging birds, insects on bark, and lizards resting on branches.

formative_check.question: Which of the following is an example of an animal using a tree for shelter?
options: A fish swimming in a pond
A bird building a nest on a sturdy branch
A rock sitting on the ground
A cloud making rain
formative_check.explanation: Trees provide physical shelter, shade, and protection from predators for nesting birds and small mammals.

citations: PLT Activity 22: Trees as Habitats
UTRGV Agroecology Campus Biodiversity Survey

nodes.title: Eco-Canvas: Bark Textures & Leaf Impressions
nodes.subject: Fine Arts
learning_objectives: Create tactile crayon rubbings showing distinct bark grooves of at least two native tree species.
Discuss how natural textures in the environment inspire artistic visual patterns.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Tactile Bark Gallery Creation
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students tape paper gently to tree trunks and rub sideways with crayons to produce high-contrast texture prints.

formative_check.question: What happens when you rub a crayon flat across paper pressed against rough tree bark?
options: The paper turns into wood
The raised ridges of the bark create a visible texture pattern
The tree loses its bark
The crayon disappears
formative_check.explanation: The raised ridges of the bark resist the crayon pressure, transferring the tree's unique fingerprint onto paper.

citations: PLT Activity 61: The Closer You Look
Texas Trees Foundation Cool Schools Art Series

nodes.title: Solar Energy Flow & Campus Food Webs
nodes.subject: Science
nodes.science_rtc: Energy and Matter: Cycles and Conservation
learning_objectives: Trace the flow of energy from sunlight to producers (trees), primary consumers (caterpillars), secondary consumers (birds), and decomposers (fungi/bacteria).
Construct a multi-tiered food web showing the ecological interdependence of South Texas native organisms.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Yarn Web of Life Simulation
equipment: Organism role cards (Sun, Mesquite, Texas Tortoise, Roadrunner, Decomposer)
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students stand in a circle holding organism cards, passing yarn to demonstrate energy transfers. When the 'tree' tugs the string, everyone feels the connected ecological ripple.

formative_check.question: In a campus microforest ecosystem, what is the ultimate original source of all energy?
options: Soil fertilizer
Sunlight captured by green leaves
Rainwater puddles
Decomposing leaf mulch
formative_check.explanation: Photosynthesis captures radiant solar energy and transforms it into chemical glucose, feeding the entire food web.

citations: 2024-2025 Revised Science TEKS 5.12B
PLT Activity 45: Web of Life

nodes.title: Tree Geometry: Pacing, Shade Area & Radius
nodes.subject: Mathematics
learning_objectives: Determine personal pace length (meters or feet per step) to measure real-world outdoor distances.
Calculate the approximate ground area of cooling shade cast by a campus tree using circle area approximations: Area ≈ π * r^2.
Estimate total playground square footage protected from direct solar radiation.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Ground Shade Shadow Stomp
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students measure their 10-step pace, walk out the four radii (North, South, East, West) of a tree's shadow, and compute the circular shade footprint.

formative_check.question: If a mature Cedar Elm tree casts a circular shadow with a radius of 4 meters, approximately what is its shaded cooling ground area? (Use π ≈ 3.14)
options: 12.5 sq meters
25.1 sq meters
50.2 sq meters
100.5 sq meters

citations: Texas Trees Foundation Cool Schools Math Curriculum
PLT Activity 67: How Big is Your Tree?

nodes.title: Roots of the RGV: Indigenous Ethnobotany & Mesquite
nodes.subject: Social Studies
learning_objectives: Explain how historic indigenous peoples of South Texas (Coahuiltecans and Karankawas) utilized the Honey Mesquite as a 'Tree of Life' for nutrition, medicine, tools, and shelter.
Analyze how indigenous ecological adaptation to arid climates contrasts with modern water-intensive land practices.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Mesquite Pod Inspection & Bean Grinding Demo
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students inspect ripe yellow mesquite pods, snap them to observe the high-sugar pulp, grind dried pods in a mortar, and taste natural sweet mesquite flour.

formative_check.question: Why was the Honey Mesquite tree known as a vital 'Tree of Life' for indigenous South Texas tribes?
options: It produced ripe nutrient-rich pods that could be stored and ground into sweet flour during hot dry summers
It made fast-growing paper for books
It only grew in freezing winter temperatures
It was the only tree that produced metal tools
formative_check.explanation: Mesquite bean pods provided high-protein, sweet carbohydrates without requiring irrigation, sustaining indigenous communities through harsh droughts.

citations: Tull, D. (2013) Edible and Useful Plants of Texas
UTRGV Center for Mexican American Studies Ethnobotany Archive

nodes.title: Sensory Nature Journaling & Tree Poetry
nodes.subject: ELAR
learning_objectives: Write vivid descriptive observations using sensory adjectives (sight, sound, touch, smell) while sitting under schoolyard canopy.
Compose a structured poem (Haiku, Cinquain, or Free Verse) conveying the protective feeling of tree shade on a hot Texas day.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: 15-Minute Sit Spot Writing Protocol
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students choose an individual 'Sit Spot' under a tree, remain silent for 7 minutes tuning in to wind and rustling leaves, then write a sensory reflection.

formative_check.question: Which sentence contains the strongest sensory imagery suitable for a field journal entry?
options: I saw a tree outside.
The rough, checkered mesquite bark smelled like warm cedar as rustling leaves whispered in the southern breeze.
Trees have green leaves that make shade.
It was very hot today.
formative_check.explanation: Sentence 2 uses sensory details (rough/checkered touch, warm cedar smell, whispering sound) to vividly transport the reader to the outdoor setting.

citations: PLT Activity 5: Poet-Tree
John Muir Laws Nature Journaling Curriculum

nodes.title: Beat the Heat: Thermoregulation, Hydration & Shade
nodes.subject: Health & PE
nodes.science_rtc: Cause and Effect: Mechanism and Explanation
learning_objectives: Explain how the human body cools itself through perspiration and how extreme humidity slows evaporation.
Compare surface temperatures between unshaded blacktop asphalt and shaded grass beneath tree canopies.
Identify the warning signs of heat exhaustion (dizziness, nausea, heavy sweating) and formulate an outdoor play safety plan.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Infrared Surface Temperature Audit
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students aim IR guns at three zones: blacktop basketball court, exposed synthetic turf, and grass beneath a dense tree canopy, recording 30°F+ differences.

formative_check.question: If the asphalt playground surface reaches 135°F at 1:00 PM, what is the best proactive health strategy for students?
options: Run faster on the blacktop
Move physical activities to the shaded microforest lawn and drink water frequently
Wear heavy black jackets
Stop drinking water
formative_check.explanation: Moving to tree shade dramatically reduces radiant thermal load, while hydration replaces fluids lost to cooling sweat.

citations: Texas DSHS Heat Safety in Schools Guide
UTRGV Cool Schools Public Health Brief

nodes.title: Photosynthesis Thermodynamics & Carbon Sequestration
nodes.subject: Science
nodes.science_rtc: Energy and Matter: Cycles and Conservation
learning_objectives: Write and balance the chemical equation for oxygenic photosynthesis: 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + light -> C6H12O6 + 6 O2.
Calculate the annual carbon storage mass in kilograms for a tree given its DBH (Diameter at Breast Height) using USDA Forest Service allometric formulas.
Explain how urban microforests act as regional carbon sinks offsetting greenhouse gas emissions.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Tree Carbon Vault Calculator
equipment: Tree DBH calipers or flexible forestry diameter tapes
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students measure DBH at 4.5 feet off the ground, look up allometric multipliers for Honey Mesquite or Live Oak, and calculate total metric kilograms of sequestered carbon.

formative_check.question: Where does the vast majority of the physical dry biomass (wood, branches, trunk) of a 10-year-old tree originate?
options: From solid minerals absorbed through the dirt
From carbon dioxide gas captured directly from the surrounding air through stomata
From water droplets absorbed during heavy thunderstorms
From commercial chemical fertilizer
formative_check.explanation: Trees build their solid cellular cellulose and lignin skeletons out of carbon atoms extracted directly from atmospheric CO2 gas during photosynthesis.

citations: USDA Forest Service i-Tree Eco Equations
Nowak et al. (2006) Carbon Storage and Sequestration

nodes.title: Microclimate Thermodynamics & Albedo Effects
nodes.subject: Science
nodes.science_sep: Planning and Carrying Out Controlled Investigations
learning_objectives: Define albedo (reflectance coefficient) and explain how dark asphalt (albedo ~ 0.08) absorbs more shortwave solar radiation than vegetative canopies (albedo ~ 0.22).
Differentiate between latent heat flux (evapotranspirative cooling) and sensible heat flux (hot surface radiant warming).
Map thermal contours across a campus using digital temperature probes.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Campus Urban Heat Island Micro-Transect
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students walk a 200-meter transect from the parking lot into the center of the Cool Schools microforest, recording ambient air temp, surface temp, and relative humidity every 25 meters.

formative_check.question: How do tree leaves physically cool ambient air compared to a canvas shade sail?
options: Leaves blow fans with their branches
Leaves undergo evapotranspiration, converting liquid water to water vapor and absorbing sensible heat as latent heat
Leaves are made of cold ice crystals
Leaves absorb all oxygen from the atmosphere
formative_check.explanation: Unlike inert canvas, living trees transpire gallons of water daily through stomata; the phase change from liquid to vapor actively chills surrounding ambient air.

citations: Oke, T. R. (1987) Boundary Layer Climates
Texas Trees Foundation Urban Heat Study

nodes.title: Forestry Trigonometry: Clinometers & Tangent Ratios
nodes.subject: Mathematics
nodes.theme_plt_label: How Do We Sustain Our Forests?
learning_objectives: Construct a functioning cardboard clinometer using a protractor, weighted string, and sighting straw.
Apply right-triangle trigonometry principles: Height = (Distance to tree * tan(Angle)) + Eye Height.
Estimate the projected 10-year timber and shade growth of native schoolyard saplings.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: DIY Clinometer Height Sweep
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students stand exactly 15 meters from a tree base, sight the top branch through the clinometer straw, read the zenith angle, and solve for total tree height.

formative_check.question: A student stands 10 meters away from a Live Oak. Her clinometer reads 45°. If her eye height is 1.4 meters, how tall is the tree? (tan 45° = 1.0)
options: 10.0 meters
11.4 meters
14.0 meters
15.4 meters
formative_check.explanation: Height = (Distance * tan 45°) + Eye Height = (10 * 1.0) + 1.4 = 11.4 meters.

citations: Texas A&M Forest Service Measuring Trees Field Guide
PLT Activity 67

nodes.title: Urban Hydrology: Infiltration, Runoff & Root Porosity
nodes.subject: Science
learning_objectives: Measure soil percolation and hydraulic conductivity rates in compacted turf versus mulched tree basins.
Explain how tree roots create macro-pores in heavy clay soils, preventing localized campus flooding during subtropical flash storms.
Calculate rainfall volume intercepted by tree leaves before reaching stormwater drains.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Coffee-Can Soil Infiltration Infiltrometer Lab
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students pound cylinders 5 cm into soil under dense trees versus exposed sports fields, pour 500 mL of water, and time the infiltration rate.

formative_check.question: Why does rainwater soak into soil much faster under a mature tree canopy than on an open turf lawn?
options: Trees attract magnets in the water
Root channels and organic leaf mulch create macro-pores that increase soil permeability and prevent soil compaction
Turf grass has deeper taproots than trees
Tree leaves boil the water into steam
formative_check.explanation: Tree roots break up compacted clay, and decomposing leaf litter creates spongy organic loam that rapidly absorbs stormwater.

citations: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service Soil Health Guide
i-Tree Hydro Technical Manual

nodes.title: Urban Agroecology & Tamaulipan Native Polycultures
nodes.subject: Science
nodes.theme_plt_label: How Do We Sustain Our Forests?
learning_objectives: Evaluate the ecological resilience of multi-strata polycultures (canopy, sub-canopy, thornscrub, groundcover) compared to monoculture turf grass.
Analyze nitrogen-fixation mechanisms in leguminous Fabaceae species (Honey Mesquite, Texas Ebony, Retama) that enrich depleted urban soils without synthetic inputs.
Design a multi-tiered food forest layout tailored to the subtropical, semi-arid Rio Grande Valley biome.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Root Nodule & Polyculture Layer Audit
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students catalog vertical canopy layers in a microforest zone and extract gentle root samples of wild legumes to identify Rhizobium bacterial nodules.

formative_check.question: How do native leguminous trees like Texas Ebony (*Ebenopsis ebano*) naturally fertilize poor urban soils?
options: They absorb nitrogen through leaf stomata
They harbor symbiotic *Rhizobium* bacteria in root nodules that fix atmospheric N2 into bioavailable ammonium (NH4+)
They manufacture synthetic chemical pellets
They kill surrounding weeds with poison
formative_check.explanation: Symbiotic bacteria in legume root nodules convert inert atmospheric N2 gas into nitrogen compounds that nourish the tree and adjacent plants.

citations: Gliessman, S. R. (2014) Agroecology: The Ecology of Sustainable Food Systems
UTRGV Agroecology Research Program

nodes.title: Environmental Justice, Redlining & Urban Heat Equity
nodes.subject: Social Studies
nodes.science_rtc: Cause and Effect: Mechanism and Explanation
learning_objectives: Analyze historical correlations between 20th-century municipal zoning, disinvestment, and modern tree canopy deficits in underserved neighborhoods.
Interpret GIS demographic layers showing higher daytime surface temperatures in low-income school districts across the Texas border region.
Draft a data-driven civic proposal for municipal shade equity and tree planting investments.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Neighborhood Canopy Disparity Mapping
equipment: Laptops/Tablets with ArcGIS StoryMaps / Google Earth Engine
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students analyze satellite vegetation indices (NDVI) across Hidalgo County zip codes and correlate canopy percentage against household income and pediatric asthma rates.

formative_check.question: What is a primary systemic cause of the 'tree canopy deficit' observed in many lower-income urban neighborhoods?
options: Trees refuse to grow in certain soils
Decades of inequitable municipal infrastructure investment, redlining, and lack of green space zoning
Residents in low-income areas dislike trees
Lower-income neighborhoods receive less total sunlight
formative_check.explanation: Historical redlining and unequal capital allocation produced neighborhoods with dense pavement and minimal municipal tree planting programs.

citations: Hoffman et al. (2020) The Effects of Historical Housing Policies on Resident Exposure to Intra-Urban Heat
Texas Trees Foundation Dallas Urban Forest Study

nodes.title: Advanced Biomass Allometry & i-Tree Engine Mathematics
nodes.subject: Mathematics
nodes.theme_plt_label: How Do We Sustain Our Forests?
learning_objectives: Formulate non-linear power-law and logarithmic regression equations modeling tree dry biomass: ln(M) = a + b*ln(DBH).
Calculate annual volumetric growth increment and calculate economic ecosystem service valuation using standard carbon offset market pricing ($/metric ton CO2e).
Perform sensitivity analysis on tree mortality versus canopy replacement timelines over a 10-year cycle.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Campus Whole-Forest Biomass Census
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students survey 25 trees on campus, measure exact DBH and crown spread, compute dry biomass in kilograms, and monetize their annual air pollution filtration value.

formative_check.question: If an allometric equation for Honey Mesquite is ln(M) = -2.13 + 2.45*ln(DBH), what happens to predicted dry biomass M if DBH doubles?
options: Biomass exactly doubles (increases by 2x)
Biomass increases non-linearly by approximately 2^2.45 ≈ 5.46 times
Biomass stays constant
Biomass decreases
formative_check.explanation: Because power-law scaling has an exponent greater than 2, a doubling of trunk diameter produces a more than five-fold increase in structural mass and carbon.

citations: Chave et al. (2014) Improved allometric models to estimate the aboveground biomass of tropical forests
USDA Forest Service General Technical Report

nodes.title: Sombra Sana: Backyard Shade Placement & Energy Savings
nodes.subject: Interdisciplinary
nodes.theme_plt_label: How Do We Sustain Our Forests?
learning_objectives: Determine optimal yard placement (South and West facing walls) to block intense afternoon solar radiant heat on residential homes.
Calculate estimated monthly electricity bill savings (15-25% reduction in AC load) from mature native shade trees.
Master the 'champagne glass' planting technique ensuring the root flare is never buried.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Community Tree Planting Demonstration
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Workshop participants work together to dig a planting hole 3x wider than the root ball, position the tree with root flare 1 inch above grade, and apply a 3-inch doughnut mulch ring.

formative_check.question: Which side of a South Texas home receives the most intense, heating afternoon sunlight in July and August?
options: The North-facing wall
The West-facing wall
The East-facing wall at sunrise
Directly under the foundation
formative_check.explanation: West-facing exterior walls absorb punishing afternoon solar radiation when outdoor ambient temperatures peak, making West-side shade trees the most effective for lowering electric bills.

citations: Texas Trees Foundation Residential Energy Study
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension Tree Care Guide

nodes.title: Agua y Vida: Water-Wise Olla & Drip Irrigation
nodes.subject: Interdisciplinary
nodes.theme_plt_label: How Do We Sustain Our Forests?
learning_objectives: Construct low-cost sub-surface clay pot (olla) irrigation systems using unglazed terracotta pots.
Explain how soil moisture tension draws water through micro-porous terracotta walls only when surrounding soil is dry, achieving 70%+ water savings compared to sprinklers.
Establish an emergency drought watering schedule for young neighborhood trees.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: DIY Olla Pot Assembly & Soil Burying Workshop
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Participants seal pot drain holes with silicone, bury the olla up to its neck adjacent to a young sapling root zone, fill with water, and cover with a lid.

formative_check.question: Why is sub-surface olla irrigation significantly more efficient than overhead lawn sprinklers in South Texas?
options: Ollas purify water with electricity
Water is released directly underground at the root zone with zero loss to surface air evaporation or wind drift
Terracotta pots make rain clouds form
Ollas use saltwater
formative_check.explanation: Because water is released below ground only when soil tension demands it, evaporation loss is virtually zero.

citations: Fanslow et al. (2018) Ancient Irrigation in Modern Arid Zones
UTRGV Agroecology Water Conservation Lab

nodes.title: La Cocina del Monte: Mesquite Pod Milling & Foraging
nodes.subject: Interdisciplinary
nodes.science_sep: Obtaining and Communicating Traditional Ecological Knowledge
learning_objectives: Identify and safely harvest ripe, golden, crisp Honey Mesquite bean pods (pechita) during dry summer months.
Demonstrate the process of drying, hammer-milling, and sifting mesquite flour.
Prepare nutrient-dense, naturally sweet, low-glycemic traditional recipes (atole, mesquite energy bars).

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Community Pechita Harvest & Milling Bee
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Participants harvest clean pods from verified campus trees, test snap crispness, run pods through the mill, sift out fibrous seed coats, and package aromatic flour.

formative_check.question: What is a key nutritional benefit of wild-harvested Honey Mesquite flour for families managing blood sugar?
options: It contains pure high-fructose corn syrup
It is naturally sweet yet rich in soluble dietary fiber and protein with a low glycemic index
It contains artificial chemical sweeteners
It has zero calories
formative_check.explanation: Mesquite flour contains complex polysaccharides and dietary fiber that slow carbohydrate absorption, preventing sharp blood sugar spikes.

citations: Tull, D. (2013) Edible and Useful Plants of Texas
Native Plant Society of Texas (NPSOT) South Texas Chapter

nodes.title: Low-Cost PM2.5 Sensor Metrology & Empirical RH Correction
nodes.subject: Environmental Engineering & Public Health
nodes.theme_plt_label: How Do We Sustain Our Forests?
nodes.science_sep: Analyzing and Interpreting Complex Data Sets
learning_objectives: Analyze the optical light-scattering physics of laser particle counters (Plantower PMS5003 / PurpleAir).
Derive hygroscopic growth correction curves when relative humidity exceeds 70%: PM2.5_cal = PM2.5_raw / (1 + a*(RH/(100-RH))^b).
Co-locate low-cost monitors with state reference stations (TCEQ CAMS 80) and compute linear regression coefficients (R^2, RMSE).

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Sensor Calibration & Data Pipeline Deployment
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Graduate researchers log 7 days of 1-minute raw sensor stream, filter humidity spikes, run non-linear regression, and deploy calibrated time-series feeds to the dashboard.

formative_check.question: Why do uncalibrated low-cost optical particulate sensors report artificially high PM2.5 mass concentrations during humid morning hours in the Rio Grande Valley?
options: Lasers lose power in humidity
Hygroscopic aerosols absorb ambient water vapor, swelling in diameter and scattering more laser light which the algorithm misinterprets as solid particulate mass
Moisture shorts out the electronic circuit board
Trees release heavy smoke in the morning
formative_check.explanation: Hygroscopic particles grow in size due to water condensation, scattering more light and leading uncorrected algorithms to over-estimate actual solid dry mass.

citations: Morawska et al. (2018) Atmospheric Environment
EPA Air Sensor Guidebook (2021)

nodes.title: Microclimate Energy Budgets & Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature Modeling
nodes.subject: Atmospheric Physics & Agroecology
nodes.science_rtc: Energy and Matter: Fluxes and Conservation
learning_objectives: Model outdoor thermal comfort using the full Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature equation: WBGT = 0.7*Tnw + 0.2*Tg + 0.1*Tdb.
Quantify sensible heat flux reduction beneath a dense microforest canopy versus bare synthetic playground surfaces.
Calculate the mean radiant temperature (Tmrt) reduction achieved by multi-species thornscrub canopy foliage.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: High-Precision Micrometeorological Mast Profiling
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Researchers set up paired stations over asphalt and microforest canopy, measuring continuous 1-second solar radiation, wind speed, dry-bulb, natural wet-bulb, and black globe metrics.

formative_check.question: In the standard WBGT formula, why is natural wet-bulb temperature (Tnw) given the highest weighting (70%)?
options: It measures the temperature of rain
It directly reflects the human body's physiological limit to cool itself through evaporative sweat dissipation in humid conditions
It is the easiest sensor to manufacture
It measures wind speed
formative_check.explanation: Tnw reflects evaporative potential; when air is hot and saturated with moisture, sweat cannot evaporate, representing the greatest physiological risk for heat stroke.

citations: Liljegren et al. (2008) Modeling the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature
UT Southwestern Medical Center Pediatric Heat Study

nodes.title: Spatial Epidemiology & Pediatric Heat-Health Vulnerability
nodes.subject: Environmental Epidemiology
teks_codes: UTRGV School of Medicine / Public Health PUBH 6310
nodes.science_rtc: Cause and Effect: Mechanism and Explanation
learning_objectives: Design an IRB-compliant, FERPA-adherent spatial epidemiological study investigating pediatric emergency department admissions for heat and asthma in Hidalgo County.
Conduct spatial bivariate Moran's I analysis correlating Landsat 9 surface thermal anomalies with school district absenteeism rates.
Evaluate the public health return-on-investment (ROI) of targeted urban afforestation in reducing pediatric thermal morbidity.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Geospatial Epidemiological Vulnerability Synthesis
equipment: Aggregated Texas DSHS health surveillance data
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Graduate researchers construct a multivariate regression model assessing whether a 10% increase in school campus canopy coverage is associated with a statistically significant decline in heat-related sick absences.

formative_check.question: When designing an educational/public health dashboard under strict COPPA and FERPA mandates, how must pediatric health outcomes be reported?
options: With individual student names and home addresses
Exclusively as de-identified, anonymized population rates aggregated at the campus or census tract level
Only using social security numbers
No health data can ever be analyzed by researchers
formative_check.explanation: FERPA and COPPA require absolute protection of student privacy, mandating that all research data be stripped of PII and aggregated at the campus or tract level.

citations: Texas DSHS Public Health Data Policies
Harlan et al. (2006) Neighborhood Microclimates and Vulnerability

nodes.title: Shinrin-yoku: Contemplative Forest Bathing & Sensory Grounding
nodes.subject: Contemplative Ecology & Well-being
learning_objectives: Practice mindful sensory immersion (Shinrin-yoku) beneath mature campus canopy to reduce sympathetic nervous system stress.
Identify phytoncides (natural aromatic antimicrobial organic compounds) released by native evergreen and thornscrub foliage.
Cultivate personal ecological attentiveness through silent sensory grounding.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Guided 20-Minute Sensory Forest Bathing Protocol
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Participants enter the campus microforest in complete silence, focus on 5 things they can see (dappled light/komorebi), 4 things they can feel, 3 things they can hear, 2 things they can smell, and 1 slow breath.

formative_check.question: What are 'phytoncides' and how do they benefit human health during a walk through a tree canopy?
options: Artificial chemical sprays used for cleaning
Natural volatile aromatic compounds released by plants that have been shown to lower cortisol, blood pressure, and boost immune activity
Dangerous poisons produced by dead trees
Plastic microfibers floating in the air
formative_check.explanation: Trees emit phytoncides to protect themselves from fungal and insect attack; inhaling these organic aerosols has been clinically shown to reduce human stress hormones and enhance immune function.

citations: Li, Q. (2010) Shinrin-yoku (Forest Bathing) and Immune Function
Kaplan & Kaplan (1989) Attention Restoration Theory

nodes.title: The Sacred Ahuehuete: Ancient Living Witnesses of the Rio Grande
nodes.subject: Cultural Heritage & Philosophy
nodes.science_rtc: Stability and Change Over Deep Time
nodes.science_sep: Synthesizing Historical, Cultural, and Ecological Records
learning_objectives: Explore the sacred cultural status of the Montezuma Cypress (*Taxodium mucronatum* / *Ahuehuete*) across pre-Columbian Mesoamerica and the South Texas borderlands.
Reflect on individual trees as 'Living Historical Archives' that endure for 1,000+ years, witnessing centuries of human cultural transformations.
Articulate the concept of reciprocal reverence between human communities and riparian old-growth ecosystems.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Living Witness Contemplation & Tree Biography
equipment: Historical timeline cards of the Rio Grande Valley (1000 CE - Present)
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Standing before a mature Montezuma Cypress or Live Oak, participants map historical milestones that occurred during the tree's lifespan and compose an honorific biography.

formative_check.question: What does the Nahuatl name 'Ahuehuete' translate to, and why is this ancient tree revered along the Rio Grande?
options: It means 'Thorn of the Desert' and was used as a fence
It translates to 'Old Man of the Water', revered for its 1,000+ year lifespan and sacred presence along riverways
It translates to 'Fast Growing Weed'
It means 'Tree with Yellow Fruit'
formative_check.explanation: Ahuehuete signifies 'old man of the water' in Nahuatl, honoring the tree's centuries-long lifespan, massive trunk buttresses, and essential riparian ecosystem guardianship.

citations: Cavazos, R. (2016) Native Flora and Cultural Traditions of the RGV
Mexican National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) Sacred Trees Archive

nodes.title: The Seven-Generations Ethic: An Intergenerational Covenant
nodes.subject: Environmental Philosophy
learning_objectives: Articulate the Indigenous 'Seven-Generations' philosophy: evaluating current environmental actions by their impact on descendants living 150+ years in the future.
Examine the physical reality that a tree planted on a school campus today will provide its maximum shade and ecological value to students seven generations ahead.
Compose an archival 'Letter to a Student in 2176' establishing an intergenerational covenant of care.

outdoor_lab_activity.title: Seven-Generations Time Capsule & Dedication Ceremony
outdoor_lab_activity.procedure: Students write commitments to protect the young campus microforest and bury an archival dedication near a sapling to be preserved for future generations.

formative_check.question: How does the 'Seven-Generations' principle change how a community views planting an oak or cypress sapling that takes 50 years to mature?
options: It encourages people to cut down trees immediately for fast cash
It reframes tree planting as an act of selfless love and stewardship for descendants we will never meet
It suggests that only fast-growing annual weeds should be planted
It teaches that nature has no long-term value
formative_check.explanation: The Seven-Generations philosophy reminds us that our ancestors planted shade for us, and our highest ecological duty is to plant canopy for descendants far into the future.

citations: Kimmerer, R. W. (2013) Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge and the Teachings of Plants
Haudenosaunee Environmental Protection Philosophy
